contract.heading: The install contract
contribute.ask_b: There is no form, because the asking is already counted. Every search that ends in NO_SAFE_MATCH is recorded as a request for that package, so using csx and getting no answer is itself the request. The board is public and it is the project's to-do list.
contribute.ask_link: See what is being asked for
contribute.claim: Every official CodeSampleX sample is generated independently and verified by running its contract. The project does not accept sample code whose origin it cannot establish.
contribute.closed_body: A sample is worth exactly what its origin is worth. Code of unknown provenance brings a licence nobody can trace, a real chance that it belongs to somebody's employer, and no way to check where it was copied from — and unlike a wrong answer, none of that can be taken back once other people's agents have read it. The rule this project applies to search applies to contribution too: a wrong sample is worse than a missing one.
contribute.closed_heading: Why sample code is not accepted
contribute.closed_later: This may open later, and if it does it will open as a proposal rather than a donation: the package, the API, the use case and a link to the documentation — with the code still generated in a clean room and verified here.
contribute.evidence_b: csx reports which public package and version you used, whether the build or test passed, and a sanitized failure fingerprint when it did not. Source code, file paths, project names, secrets and raw logs never leave the machine — in local-only mode nothing leaves it at all. This needs no account and no identity.
contribute.lead: The samples are written and verified by CodeSampleX. Everything around them is open, and the part that actually needs other people is open first.
contribute.report_b: The most valuable report is a release note: a library fixed something, and nobody wrote down what actually changed. That becomes a regression case — the old version fails the contract, the new one passes it — and the pair is worth more than either half. Report the library, the versions, and what you saw.
contribute.source: Everything above is checkable in the source
contribute.title: How to contribute
contribute.verify_b: This is the one thing the project cannot do alone. A sample is verified on the machines that exist, and yours has a libc version, a runtime build and an OS that no amount of work here can substitute for. A second machine agreeing is what moves a sample from PUBLISHED to CROSS_PASS; the ladder is built out of other people's computers.

cube.drill_note: Cells are aggregates of everything still varying in this slice (the n/m count says how much). Click one to pin its coordinates and see the next level.

findings.capped: This list is held at its ceiling; older derived findings are not shown.
findings.filter_note: OS and runtime come from the environment recorded by the linked sample. Entries without that dimension are omitted when you select it.
findings.group_belief_note: Here the belief is migration advice, a habit carried over from a neighbouring library, or something everyone repeats. The measurement is the same kind of measurement.
findings.group_derived: Stated by the sample, measured by its contract
findings.group_derived_note: Nobody writes this group. Each entry is a published sample whose author recorded the belief it corrects, beside the first line of the contract that ran against it. It grows when samples are published, not when this page is edited — so the entries above, which are hand-checked, lead.
findings.group_docs_note: Here the belief is not folklore: it is what the project's own documentation, or the specification it implements, says. Both halves are checkable — the quote is one link away, the measurement one container run.
findings.intro: Every line below is a measurement, not an opinion. Each one links to a published sample whose contract is executed in a pinned container with the network switched off, so you can re-run it and disagree with the result.
findings.method_body: Open the sample, read its contract, run it. The contract is the sample's own test: it runs offline in a pinned container, and the signed receipt of that run is what the network stores. Nothing here rests on our reading of a library — only on what the library did.
findings.method_heading: How to check any line here
findings.method_missing: Findings whose sample could not be confirmed live are not on this page. The list is shorter than what the sample pool contains, on purpose.
findings.none: No findings match these filters. The network only shows measurements it can support.
findings.range: Showing %s–%s of %s measured by published samples.
findings.rerun: Sample ids are content addresses. GET /v1/samples/<id> returns the sample this page links to, and csx runs its contract in the same container the network verified it in.
findings.search: Search findings — a package, an API, a word from the claim
findings.title: What the network found
findings.untranslated: The page is translated; the findings are not. Each one quotes an error string, an attribute name or a numeric result, and a translated paraphrase of a measurement is no longer the measurement.

landing.agents_auto: csx init finds these and registers the MCP server for you. No config file to edit.
landing.agents_manual: Any other MCP client works too — Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, Zed, VS Code. csx is a standard stdio MCP server. Run this and paste what it prints; it fills in the absolute path of your install, which a client started by your editor will not find on its own:
landing.agents_models: Model-agnostic. The same compatibility evidence serves Claude, GPT and Codex, Gemini, Llama — any model that can call an MCP tool.
landing.findings_sub: Each line was measured by a published sample whose contract ran offline in a pinned container. Click one to read it.
landing.for_agents: Your coding agent can consume the same network through the MCP adapter: it asks CodeSampleX before writing code against a public library, and reports back whether the answer built. The CLI and the web report read identically.
landing.install_note: One command, one question. Everything else is automatic.
landing.llm_body: Paste this prompt into the coding agent you already have open. It follows the official install instructions instead of guessing them, adds csx to your MCP config, and checks the connection before it reports success.
landing.llm_clients: csx init registers Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and OpenCode by absolute path. Any other stdio MCP client is registered from what csx mcp-config prints.
landing.llm_copy_failed: Copy failed. Select the prompt and copy it manually.
landing.llm_heading: Let your coding agent install it
landing.llm_link: Or let your coding agent install it →
landing.llm_prompt:
Install the CodeSampleX (csx) MCP server for the coding agent I am using right now.

Use only the official CodeSampleX instructions — https://github.com/r2cuerdame/CodeSampleX/blob/main/llms-install.md, with the installers at %s/install.sh (macOS, Linux) and %s/install.ps1 (Windows). Do not improvise commands or config from memory.

1. Read my MCP config before you write to it. Keep every server already listed and add csx next to them; never replace the file.
2. Register csx by its absolute path — a client my editor starts does not inherit my shell PATH.
3. csx has no account: do not ask me for a token, password or API key, and do not write a secret into any config.
4. Initialize community mode with `csx init --community --yes` so this installation receives and contributes network evidence; do not leave it local-only. Only sanitized public package, version, symbol, environment and build-result facts are shared — never source, paths, project names, secrets, private packages or raw logs.
5. Verify before reporting success: confirm `csx daemon status` reports `mode: community`, run `csx sync` once, then confirm my client lists csx and that a `search_known_solution` call answers.
6. Tell me every file you changed, and anything you could not do.
landing.llm_safety: Read it before you send it. It asks for no account, token or password — csx needs none — and it tells the agent to add csx alongside the MCP servers you already have, never to overwrite your config.
landing.worker_body: For a spare machine that should contribute independent cross-verification and exact matrix verification, copy this prompt instead. It installs no MCP entry and runs the Docker-isolated worker automatically after login.
landing.worker_run_prompt:
Start and check the existing CodeSampleX Contributor Worker on this machine. Do not reinstall csx or change any MCP or coding-agent settings.

Confirm Docker is running, start the existing user service, and verify that its exact command is `csx worker start --mode verify --parallel 2 --budget idle`, the service is running, `csx version` succeeds, and `csx daemon status` is `not running`. An empty queue is normal. Report the service state and any error you could not fix safely.
landing.worker_setup_prompt:
Set up this machine as a CodeSampleX worker only. Follow only the ‘Worker-only machine’ section of https://github.com/r2cuerdame/CodeSampleX/blob/main/llms-install.md. Use %s/install.sh on macOS/Linux or %s/install.ps1 on Windows.

1. Install or upgrade csx.
2. Confirm Docker is already running; otherwise stop without installing it or requesting administrator access.
3. Run exactly `csx init --community --yes --no-agents --no-daemon`.
4. Create or update one native user service named `CodeSampleX Contributor Worker` that runs `csx worker start --mode verify --parallel 2 --budget idle`, starts after login and restarts on failure.
5. Start it and report the service state, exact command and csx version. Confirm `csx daemon status` is `not running`. Do not add MCP or inspect projects.
landing.worker_prompt:
Set up this machine as a worker-only CodeSampleX verifier. Do not connect csx to an MCP client or modify any coding-agent configuration.

Follow only the official CodeSampleX instructions at https://github.com/r2cuerdame/CodeSampleX/blob/main/llms-install.md and its Worker-only machine section. Use the installers at %s/install.sh (macOS, Linux) or %s/install.ps1 (Windows). Do not invent commands or configuration from memory.

1. Install or upgrade the csx binary and report its absolute path.
2. Confirm that a reachable Docker daemon is already available. If Docker is missing or stopped, report that and stop; do not install Docker or request administrator access without my approval.
3. Initialize exactly with `csx init --community --yes --no-agents --no-daemon`. This machine must be community mode, but worker-only: do not add an MCP server, agent rule, project hook or repository integration.
4. Using the OS-native per-user service mechanism documented there, create or update one persistent service named `CodeSampleX Contributor Worker`. It must run the absolute csx binary as `csx worker start --mode verify --parallel 2 --budget idle`, start automatically, restart on failure and avoid duplicate instances. Use no third-party scheduler.
5. Start it now and verify both that the service is active and that `csx daemon status` reports `not running`. An empty queue is healthy and must not be reported as a failure.
6. Report the service name, process state, exact command, every file or task changed, and anything you could not complete.

The worker may accept only server-assigned VERIFY jobs with reason=cross or reason=matrix, and only when every exact job requirement maps to an environment its pinned local runner can prepare. For matrix work, keep the downloaded content-addressed artifact immutable and overlay only the requested execution environment onto an in-memory manifest copy. Run the artifact only in disposable Docker workspaces, never directly on the host, and do not read local project source.
landing.worker_safety: Worker-only means exactly that: community mode plus a Docker verifier. It does not register MCP or inspect projects. Docker installation and administrator access still require your approval.
landing.scope_note: Evidence is not limited to libraries. SDKs, runtimes, OS commands, and CLIs such as npm, Maven, and Git use the same contracts and measured results.
landing.tested_line: Tested across real environments. Not guessed from documentation.
landing.matrix_sub: A live slice of one measured package's compatibility cube. Click any cell to drill into that slice; every number is a recorded run, not an estimate.
landing.matrix_trimmed: Showing the environments with the most evidence.
landing.matrix_empty: The first compatibility grids appear here as soon as the network records enough environment evidence.
landing.samples_heading: Then how do I use it?
landing.samples_sub: Verified answers: each one ran in a pinned container with the network off and passed its own contract before publication.
landing.ladder_sub: Every result carries its evidence class. The ladder goes up only by doing more, never by claiming more.
landing.ladder_observed: A real project built, typechecked or tested with the package — observed, not proof that one API works.
landing.ladder_verified: A sample's own contract ran in a pinned container with the network off, and passed.
landing.ladder_cross: An independent peer re-ran the same sample and its contract passed again.
landing.ladder_multi: Passing runs span at least two OS, runtime or browser boundaries.
landing.ladder_stable: At least three independent peers pass it and no failure was recorded for 30 days.
landing.ladder_rule: Observations and verifications are never summed: a project compiling is never presented as an API working. Evidence older than 90 days counts as stale and says so.
landing.legend_pass: PASS — every verification in this slice passed
landing.legend_fail: FAIL — every verification in this slice failed
landing.legend_mixed: MIXED — passes and failures in this slice
landing.legend_observed: OBSERVED — build observations only, no contract run
landing.legend_bang: measured anomaly: elevated failure rate or a failing verification
landing.legend_maybe: weak or aged evidence: observation-only, or older than 90 days (stale)
landing.legend_cross: cross-checked by at least two independent peers

landing.cli_can_search: ask for a verified answer graded against your environment
landing.cli_can_scan: record which public packages a project uses, without building
landing.cli_can_stats: your local dashboard: hits, adoptions, queue
landing.agents_role: MCP is how coding agents consume the same network — an adapter over the CLI and API, not a separate product.
landing.value_1_b: Minimal samples verified by a contract in a clean sandbox — not a snippet someone hoped would work.
landing.value_2_b: Every result is rated against your versions, runtime and execution context — Node, browser, WebView, Electron, worker.
landing.value_3_b: Where it broke, how often, and the likely cause as a probability — never a made-up certainty.
landing.what_a: Official docs can't answer that. Recorded runs from real machines can.
landing.what_body: CodeSampleX tests developer tools across real environments. Builds and contract runs on real machines become anonymous evidence; verified samples prove specific APIs in pinned containers; cross-checks and multi-environment runs harden the result. The map you browse here is the record of what actually happened — and your coding agent can ask it before writing code.
landing.what_q: Will this API actually work with my package, version, and runtime combination?

sample.evidence_intro: Declared environment and signed verification runs are separated so you can see exactly what this sample proves.
sample.environment_missing: This environment was not recorded; nothing is inferred.
sample.status_help: Publication state. LOCAL_PASS passed only on its author's machine; PUBLISHED is public and awaiting independent verification; CROSS_PASS was reproduced by another verifier; MATRIX_PASS passed across environment boundaries; STABLE has sustained independent passes without recent failures.
sample.level_help: Evidence strength. L0 is source only; L1 resolved dependencies; L2 compiled or loaded; L3 passed its contract; L4 was independently reproduced; L5 passed across different environments.

stats.verified_samples_sub: usable answers that passed their contract
stats.how_1: You build or test through csx — or your coding agent does it for you.
stats.how_2: Your machine works out which public packages, versions and API symbols were involved, and which stage passed or failed.
stats.how_3: Errors are reduced to fingerprints locally. Paths, project names, secrets and raw logs never leave your machine.
stats.how_4: Anonymous evidence batches build the public compatibility map you are browsing here.
stats.how_5: Your agent asks CodeSampleX first and gets the closest verified sample plus the exact difference from your environment.

stats.how_intro: Every number above comes out of this loop. None of it is a guess about your code — it is what actually happened in real development environments.

support.gradle_java_note: Gradle contract verification supports exact Java 8, 11, 17 and 21 on Gradle 8.14.3, and Java 25 on Gradle 9.7.0; all use Corretto on Amazon Linux 2023/glibc. Sample Gradle projects and local Java project scanning are not supported.
support.maven_java_note: Maven contract verification keeps omitted Java at the legacy Java 21 Temurin Alpine/musl default, and supports exact Java 8, 11, 17, 21 and 25 on Maven 3.9.11 with Corretto on Amazon Linux 2023/glibc. Local Java project scanning is not yet supported.
support.verification_only_note: Verified public samples are supported. Local project scanning is not yet supported.
symbol.callshape_note: These counts do not distinguish how the symbol was called: overloads, argument shapes and options are pooled together. What a particular call shape does is proven by a sample's contract, not by these numbers.
symbol.evidence_note: Project-level observations and symbol/contract verifications are counted separately and never combined.
version.matrix_sub: Symbols × operating systems for this version. Cells drill into the package's compatibility cube.
wanted.contribute: A row leaves this list the moment a verified sample answers it. Samples are written and verified by CodeSampleX, so this is the project's to-do list rather than yours — but the list itself is built from what people asked for and could not get, which is the part only you can supply.
wanted.empty: Nothing is being asked for yet.
wanted.empty_why: This list is built from real misses reported by real installs. An empty board means no one has hit a question the network could not answer — which, this early, means almost nobody has asked one.
wanted.intro: Questions the network had no answer for, most-asked first. Every other page here describes what exists; this one is the list of what nobody has written down yet.
wanted.privacy: The questions themselves are not here and never will be. A typed question carries project names and file paths, so it stays on the machine that asked. What is counted is the package — public before anyone asked about it — and one reporter counts once a day, so nobody can push something up the list by asking twice.
